Franklin saw that Bradford, by asking artful questions and raising little doubts, drew Keimer into explaining all his plans. Listening quietly while others talk can reveal far more than talking yourself.
Franklin fixed the broken press and got the shop ready before doing the job asked of him. Taking care of the basic tools of your trade first makes everything you do afterwards possible.

Franklin judged the two printers by their real skills, noting that one was untrained and the other knew composing but not presswork. Be honest about where your own skills stop, and find people who fill those gaps.
Franklin kept his own counsel while building a new life, sharing his whereabouts only with a trusted friend. Discretion about your plans can protect them until they are ready.
Franklin's reasoning, as he tells it, shows that a clear, fair letter can change how others see you. Explaining your reasons calmly and fully can win over someone who first thought you were mistaken.

Franklin's account suggests that people with influence often open doors for capable young workers who show promise. Being willing to be seen and to accept an invitation can turn a quiet skill into real opportunity.
Franklin met a rough return with composure, arriving well presented and with savings in hand, which spoke for him more than words could. Steady progress often answers doubters better than argument.

Franklin's father judged that a youth should not be set up in business before he is mature enough to manage it, since a business needs careful handling and preparation. Showing off one's possessions to others can also build resentment, as his brother's anger shows.

Franklin's father advised that steady industry and prudent saving, rather than borrowing or help from others, would build a young man's start in business. He also urged him to earn general esteem and avoid mocking or slandering others.

Franklin took the advice of an older, experienced stranger who warned him about company that seemed pleasant but was dangerous. Heeding a sensible warning about people, even when they seem friendly, saved him from theft and worse.
Benjamin Franklin saw that a friend who was gifted and promising could still be undone by one habit, drink, which turned his talents to waste. Watch for the slow decline in people you care about.

Franklin learned that lending money to a friend who keeps promising to repay, while having no income to show for it, can leave you exposed. Be careful about how much you let someone borrow from you when their prospects are unclear.
Franklin held that anger and a sour mood cloud judgment, so a small quarrel can grow into a bigger one than it needs to be. Notice when your own feelings are steering your decisions.

Franklin found that an offer of help can look generous and sincere while hiding a habit of making promises that are never kept. Check a person's reputation with others before you rely on their word, especially when you are depending on it.

Benjamin Franklin saw that going to the source in person, choosing your own stock and meeting the people in your trade, can pay off in useful contacts and better goods. Being on the spot often beats ordering from afar.
Benjamin Franklin noticed how easily a reasonable mind can find a reason for whatever it already wants to do. Be wary of building arguments to suit your appetite.
Benjamin Franklin used a Socratic method of patient questions that led an opponent step by step into contradictions. It works best when you ask, not when you lecture, and it wins people over.
Benjamin Franklin observed that a sudden change of habit often sits easier than a slow, gradual one. He also warned that a plan you have lost interest in is easily abandoned when temptation arrives.

Benjamin Franklin noticed that Osborne's advice to Ralph was sound: steady diligence and punctuality can earn a start in business, even without capital. Ralph, by contrast, was chasing a dream that was unlikely to pay.

Franklin passed off Ralph's poem as his own and let his friends judge it on its merits. Praise for work that is unsigned or unclaimed shows what people really think of it, and it humbled Osborne's habit of criticising too freely.

Franklin's tale of the governor shows how a promise of help that keeps being postponed can leave a person stranded. Ask for a firm date and written commitments before you plan around someone else's word.

Benjamin Franklin learned to check claims before relying on them: he compared the letters he was given with what he knew of the sender. Trust should follow evidence about a person's character, not just a polite manner.

Benjamin Franklin took his setback to a trusted, experienced friend, who advised him to improve his skills in his own trade while in London. A setback can become a chance to build the skills you will need later.
Benjamin Franklin observed that a man who wishes to please everybody, and has little to give, ends up giving only expectations. Promises that cannot be kept do lasting damage to trust.

Benjamin Franklin passed on information to Hamilton, who was in a position to use it, even though it was not in his own interest to make a fuss. Telling a person what affects them is a fair and useful thing to do.

Franklin saw that his friend Ralph kept chasing jobs that were beneath his pride, and so kept failing. Being willing to take honest, modest work while looking for something better is a sound way to get by.

Franklin called his own choices like neglecting a far-off obligation and printing a provocative pamphlet his 'errata', and wished he could correct them. Owning past mistakes plainly, without excuse, is a useful habit.
Franklin got ahead by making himself useful to people and by showing a curious, willing mind, so new acquaintances opened doors. Good work and an open manner tend to bring useful contacts.

books.title: The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
books.author: Charles Darwin
books.subject: emotions
books.licence_note: Author died 1882. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Charles Darwin held that many expressions come from habits that once served a purpose, such as the three chief principles he sets out in the first chapter. Expressions can outlast the reason they first existed.

Charles Darwin's principle of antithesis suggests that opposite moods often show up as opposite postures. A relaxed, friendly stance is often the reverse of a hostile one, and people read these signals without being taught.
Charles Darwin noticed that the body reacts to strong feelings without waiting for the will. Blushing, trembling and changes in the skin show what someone feels even when they try to hide it.

Charles Darwin observed that people of very different backgrounds show many of the same expressions. Recognising a face or gesture is largely instinctive, so most of us can read a stranger's mood without a shared language.

Charles Darwin noted that Sir Charles Bell's real service was showing how the movements of expression are tied to breathing. He also showed that the muscles round the eyes tighten during hard breathing out, to protect the eyes.

Charles Darwin held that a list of how a face looks is not enough; a good account must also explain why each muscle moves as it does under each feeling. Flowery descriptions that never explain the cause add little understanding.

Charles Darwin warned that confident explanations which are really just fancy can be worse than none. He quoted Le Brun's theory of fright as an example of nonsense dressed up as science, so claims should be tested, not admired.

Darwin praised Duchenne for studying each facial muscle closely and for showing which muscles are hardest to control by the will. He also noted that a careful researcher can be right even when some of his claims are overstated.

Darwin held that many gestures, like a billiards player nudging a wayward ball, come from long habit: we repeat the body movements that once worked, even when they no longer do anything. Habit can explain behaviour that looks purposeless.

Darwin suggested that a dog's pricked ears and fixed gaze are linked because the two actions were repeated together for many generations. A simpler habit-based explanation is often better than a mystical idea of sympathy between body parts.
Charles Darwin noted that Bain saw expression as part of feeling itself, a general spreading of excitement through the body. Darwin judged this too broad to explain any particular expression.

Charles Darwin held that many expressions grow out of the actions that feeling would naturally bring on, such as the cries, tremblings and tensed muscles of fear. Spencer's law is that strong feeling spills over into bodily action along the most habitual nerve routes.

Charles Darwin argued that a feature shared with other species, such as the facial muscles we have in common with apes, is unlikely to exist only for display. Before assuming a single purpose, look for the other jobs a thing might do.

Darwin argued that animals, like the dog greeting its master, show real emotional expression, so claiming it is only instinct or will is too narrow a view. Careful observation should replace a quick assumption that the matter is settled.

Darwin held that if each species is seen as a separate creation, the question of why we show emotions is closed off and nothing is really explained. Viewing all creatures as gradually changing from common ancestors opens up useful investigation.

Darwin warned that sympathy during a strong emotion and our own expectations both make careful observation harder, since we easily see what we expect to see. He recommended watching infants first, because they show feelings more plainly than adults.

Darwin held that the best way to learn about extreme emotion was to study people who give their feelings uncontrolled vent, and he gained much from an expert who shared notes freely. Learning from a generous specialist can speed up your own understanding.

Darwin found that viewers who saw photographs without any explanation disagreed widely about what the faces showed. He also saw that once he read the intended meaning, he judged the pictures far more truthful, showing how easily our imagination misleads us.

Darwin reasoned that if the same expression appears across very different peoples, it is probably natural rather than learned, since learned gestures would vary like languages do. Look for patterns that hold across different groups before trusting a conclusion.

Darwin asked his questions in a way that favoured actual observation over memory, and he admitted later that his queries could have been much better written. When gathering evidence, ask for what people have directly seen, and be willing to say your method could be improved.
Charles Darwin held that answers resting on a written record of the circumstances and the expression itself deserve more trust than bare yes or no replies. Vague general remarks count for less.

Charles Darwin held that watching animals is a safer guide than watching people, since animals are less shaped by imagination or convention. Their expressions give a firmer basis for working out where behaviours come from.

Charles Darwin held that observing expressions is hard, because fleeting changes, distraction, imagination and long familiarity all bias what we think we see. He stressed checking what we believe against careful evidence.

Charles Darwin held that a theory is best tested by checking whether the same principle also explains related cases, including animals as well as people. A good idea should hold up across the wider evidence.

Charles Darwin held that a question should be approached with a fresh view once a working belief forms, so he reframed each expression as something needing its own rational explanation rather than accepting a fixed answer.
Darwin's approach was to test an idea by gathering many careful observations from people across different places, not by relying on a single authority's account.
Darwin noted that people often hide their feelings around strangers, so observers must be patient and trusted before they can read what is really going on.
Darwin valued a habit of careful, detailed observation, showing that a skill built in one field, such as botany, can sharpen judgement in another.

Charles Darwin noted that the facial muscles vary a great deal from one person to another, in both their structure and what they can do. So any single textbook picture only describes the typical case.

Charles Darwin held that useful actions tied to a state of mind become habits, so they keep happening under that state even when they no longer serve any purpose. Muscles least under the will are the most likely to slip out.
Charles Darwin held that when a directly opposite state of mind arises, we tend to make movements that are the opposite of the earlier ones, even though those movements do no good.
Darwin held that habit makes complex movements easy over time, and that repeated use can even be passed on to offspring, as with trained gaits in horses and pointing in young dogs.

Darwin noted that an inherited tendency often needs some practice in the individual before it works well, since young dogs may point at the wrong scent. Good results depend on both inheritance and experience.

Darwin quoted Bain's principle that actions and feelings occurring together tend to become linked, so that one later brings the other to mind. Many everyday habits, like putting on gloves without thinking, come from this.

Darwin observed that people often scratch their heads, rub their eyes or cough when perplexed or embarrassed, as if relieving a small discomfort. Many of our habits are small ways of responding to our own inner states.

Darwin noted that we often shut our eyes or turn away from things we reject, and raise our eyebrows when trying to remember something, even when there is nothing to see. Our bodies tend to act out our thinking in ways we rarely notice.

Darwin observed that we often copy or mirror the movements of people around us, such as clearing our throats when a singer is hoarse. Much of what we do in company is driven by imitation and sympathy rather than deliberate choice.

Darwin explained that many actions, such as coughing and sneezing, happen without thought, and even a decapitated frog can wipe off acid with a leg. Some behaviour that looks intelligent runs on automatic nerve responses.

Darwin observed that acts we perform by will are often weaker and slower than the same acts done by reflex, because the conscious mind takes time and effort to act. Deliberate effort can get in the way of what the body does best.
Darwin's wager showed that a strong wish to succeed can stop a natural reflex from working. Trying too hard at a simple, automatic act can make it harder to do well.

Darwin found that resolving calmly not to flinch failed the moment a threat seemed real, because reason alone cannot override what the imagination believes is danger. Fear is often stronger than logic, so plan for that rather than trusting willpower alone.
Darwin observed that his infants started at sudden sounds but did not blink, and he reasoned that a reflex learned by experience over many generations could be passed on before it is needed.
Darwin suggested that some actions first done on purpose, such as expelling an irritant by sneezing or coughing, can become automatic reflexes over long habit and inheritance.
Darwin argued that some reflexes, such as the iris narrowing in bright light, cannot have been learned by the will and fixed by habit, so they need a different explanation.
Darwin held that reflexes, like other bodily traits, vary slightly, and useful variations tend to be kept and passed on, so a reflex built for one purpose can later be adapted to another.

Charles Darwin held that many habits are inherited movements that once served a purpose, such as a dog turning round to flatten grass. Such habits are often repeated long after they have stopped being useful.

Darwin observed that a habit can be triggered by circumstances where it no longer fits, such as a dog crouching when it sees a distant stranger on an open road. Actions can outlast the situations that first gave them a point.

Darwin noticed that the dog's habit of scratching backwards after going to the toilet is a leftover from an ancestor that covered its waste, even though dogs no longer do this. Some habits are kept for a very long time without any clear use.

Darwin observed that a terrier will toss, roll on and worry a biscuit as if it were prey, which suggests that a habit can supply a feeling of value that the situation lacks. Habits can run on their own logic rather than on what the mind knows to be true.

Darwin noticed that a horse rubbed on the neck will move its jaws as if nibbling another horse, since it could never reach its own neck. Expressions can be stirred by a stimulus that the animal cannot actually act on.

Darwin observed that a habit can be set off by the wrong cue, as when a kitten scraped ashes over spilt water, or shook its feet at a sound of pouring. Routines fire on signals that look like the real trigger, not only on the real thing.

Darwin saw that a movement which began as a feeding action, kneading the mother for milk, can later become a sign of comfort, as with cats pounding a soft shawl while purring. Over time, an old action can turn into a way of showing a feeling.

Darwin noted that some useful actions, such as a chick pecking at food, can be triggered by a simple cue like a tapping sound, not by sight or smell. Many skilled habits run on a single signal, so the cue matters as much as the skill.

Charles Darwin held that a movement which once served a feeling becomes habit, and can still appear faintly when that feeling returns, even when it does no good. Under strain, the will gives way first on the muscles it controls most.

Charles Darwin held that the principle of antithesis means a strongly opposite state of mind tends to produce movements opposite to those of the first state, even when those movements serve no purpose.

Charles Darwin observed that a dog's friendly greeting is the reverse of its hostile stance: a relaxed body, lowered tail and smooth hair, where the threatening dog stands stiff and upright. Such signs are easier to read once you know the opposing state.

Charles Darwin noted that a cat's anger and its readiness to fight show in a crouch, lashing tail and flattened ears, and that a leaping predator shows much the same signs. Reading body language means comparing a creature's posture against its likely intention.
Charles Darwin noticed that a dog's gloomy look at being turned away from a walk was the opposite of its joyful bearing, showing how a small disappointment can change a whole posture at once.
Charles Darwin observed that social animals depend on being understood by one another, so gestures and expressions matter greatly to their survival and to getting along together.
Charles Darwin held that a gesture can be inherited even if it began as a deliberate act, since habits repeated over many generations may eventually become innate.

books.title: On the Origin of Species
books.author: Charles Darwin
books.subject: big ideas
books.licence_note: Author died 1882. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Charles Darwin's opening quotes hold that events come about through general laws rather than separate interventions of divine power, and that a person should keep studying both the book of God's word and the book of God's works. Keep learning widely and never stop.

Darwin observed that every species can increase far faster than its food and space allow, so competition is universal. The fiercest struggle is usually between individuals and varieties of the same species, not between different kinds of creatures.

Darwin noted that traits that are used grow stronger and those left unused tend to fade, and that changes in one part of a body often bring changes in another. Competition among small differences is what shapes which forms survive.

Darwin spent years gathering and reflecting on facts before he trusted his conclusions, and he said so openly to show he had not been hasty. Careful, patient evidence-gathering comes before a firm decision.

Darwin held back his work for years, but he chose to publish a shorter version once another researcher had reached much the same ideas. Sharing your work in time matters more than waiting for it to be perfect.
Darwin held that a conclusion about descent is unsatisfying until you can show how the modifications arose. Explaining fine adaptation by a vague outside cause is not enough.
Darwin held that the best way to understand how living things change is to study domesticated animals and cultivated plants, which show variation openly. He thought this was neglected but valuable.
Darwin held that more individuals are born than can survive, so any slight variation that helps an individual has a better chance and is passed on. Small advantages accumulate over generations.

Darwin held that our knowledge of how living things depend on one another is so limited that much about the origin of species will stay unexplained for a long time. He still saw that these relations shape the future of every living thing.

Darwin argued that species are not fixed but descend from earlier, often extinct, species, much as varieties descend from their parent species. He saw natural selection as the main, though not the only, means of change.

Darwin observed that cultivated plants and animals vary more among themselves than wild species do, likely because they are raised under less uniform conditions. A change in conditions has to last several generations before it produces noticeable variation.

Darwin suspected that most variation starts in the reproductive elements before conception, since confinement and cultivation disturb breeding far more than other bodily functions. Changes in conditions can quietly stop an organism from reproducing.

Darwin noted that 'sporting' buds, which suddenly differ from the rest of a plant, are rare in nature but common under cultivation. He took this as support for the idea that variation comes from the parent's treatment before reproduction.

Darwin observed that seedlings and young from the same parents can differ noticeably even under identical conditions. So the direct effect of food, light and climate is usually small compared with the laws of reproduction and inheritance.

Darwin held that use and disuse shape a body over generations, so a domestic duck with less flying and more walking ends up with lighter wings and heavier legs. Habit can therefore leave a lasting mark that is passed on.
Charles Darwin noted that changing one part of an animal often changes other, distinct parts too, so a breeder who selects for one trait will likely alter others without meaning to.
Charles Darwin argued that inheritance should be treated as the normal rule and non-inheritance as the exception, since rare traits that reappear in a family are unlikely to be coincidence.
Charles Darwin observed that a trait tends to show up in offspring at the same stage of life it first appeared in the parent, a rule he thought central to understanding embryology.

Darwin argued that the claim that domestic varieties always revert to wild ancestors is unproven. Reversion is possible, but the outcome depends on changed conditions, and natural selection decides which new traits survive.

Darwin held that domestic races of one species differ from each other much as closely related species do in nature, only usually to a lesser degree. Experts often disagree whether a given form is a variety or a distinct species.

Darwin noted that it is hard to measure how different domestic races are when we do not know whether they came from one parent species or several. Settling that question would bear on whether closely allied wild species are truly fixed.

Darwin doubted the idea that people chose animals and plants for domestication because they were unusually variable or hardy. Early humans could not have known such traits in advance, and any species given time under breeding would vary much as domesticated ones have.

Darwin admitted that the origin of most ancient domestic animals and plants cannot be settled, since old records show diversity that may have arisen long before those records. Ancient evidence can only show when a breed was already known, not how it began.

Darwin warned that it is absurd to assume a separate wild ancestor for every slight, true-breeding variety. Inherited variation within a species can explain much of what looks like many separate origins.

Darwin held that crossing two very different breeds rarely gives a stable new one, since the mongrels of later generations differ widely. Producing a lasting new form takes careful, long-continued selection of the best individuals.

Charles Darwin held that choosing one special group to study closely, such as domestic pigeons, is the best way to learn general truths. He kept every breed he could obtain and talked with expert fanciers.

Charles Darwin noticed that many separate features of a body, from bones to feathers to eggs, can each vary independently. Careful study means looking at all of these traits, not just the most obvious one.

Charles Darwin reasoned by testing each rival explanation against the evidence. He asked whether the supposed original stocks could still exist unnoticed, or could have vanished, and found the second story hard to believe.

Darwin held that when many unlikely coincidences must all be true for a claim to work, the claim becomes improbable in the highest degree. He weighed how many strange chances a theory needed, not just whether it could be true.

Darwin held that when a trait keeps reappearing after crossbreeding, the simplest explanation is that the birds share a common ancestor, since the trait is hidden in their family history. Competing explanations often need several improbable assumptions to hold at once.

Darwin held that when several separate pieces of evidence each point the same way, taken together they can justify a conclusion that no single piece could. He also warned against stretching a hypothesis, such as easy fertility between distinct kinds, without any direct test.

Darwin held that a claim gains strength when it is backed by many independent lines of evidence, such as a smooth series of forms, traits that vary widely within a group, and long human records. He treated careful watching and patient breeding over time as a real source of knowledge.

Darwin noticed that breeders are firmly sure their breeds came from separate species, yet they accept slight differences as they win prizes by them. He urged caution before dismissing an idea just because its steps are too small to see.

Darwin held that the great variety of useful domestic breeds comes from accumulative selection: nature supplies small variations, and people add them up in the directions they find useful, one generation at a time.

Darwin pointed out that skilled breeders treat a living form as something they can shape steadily over the years. Patient, repeated selection, judged again and again, can change a flock far more than most people expect.

Darwin observed that the real gains came from small differences, too fine for an untrained eye, piled up over many generations. Mastery needs a sharp eye, years of study and sustained perseverance, and most people will not reach it.

Darwin noted that different varieties of one plant species often differ sharply in one valued part, such as leaves, flowers or fruit, while looking nearly alike in others. Choosing one trait over generations can reshape that part alone.

Darwin argued that the principle of selection was not a modern discovery, since ancient writers and early breeders already valued it. Careful attention to what gets passed on is an old and common practice.

Darwin held that unconscious selection works quietly: each person who keeps and breeds from their best individuals slowly changes a line over time, even without meaning to. Small steady choices add up to large change.

Charles Darwin observed that small, steady choices over generations can make animals and plants very different from their origins, and that breeders following the same method can end up with two quite different strains.
Charles Darwin held that people often keep the most useful animal alive in hard times, so the best individuals leave more offspring and a quiet selection happens even without anyone intending it.
Charles Darwin argued that gardeners improved fruit and flowers by always growing and saving seed from the best plant they had, so that progress came slowly and almost unconsciously.
Charles Darwin noted that improvement built up over centuries is why the wild ancestors of many garden plants are now hard to recognise at all.

Charles Darwin held that breeders can only select from variations nature first provides, and that the breeder rarely sets out to build a final form, since the first small deviation is what catches the eye.
Charles Darwin observed that people notice very small differences and value any novelty they own, so a slight change can matter far more to a keen eye than it would to an outsider.
Charles Darwin noted that improvements usually build up slowly and unrecorded, like a dialect, so the true history of a gradual change is often lost even when its results are plain to see.
Charles Darwin argued that improvement comes from keeping many individuals and paying close attention to small differences, since useful variations appear only now and then and are easily neglected.

Darwin noted that breeders succeed more easily when they can keep different lines apart and mate animals reliably, since pigeons pair for life and can be bred quickly in numbers. Breeds only form where someone actually chooses which animals to keep and breed.

Darwin held that the accumulated effect of selection, whether done deliberately and quickly or unconsciously and slowly, is the strongest force shaping change. Many other causes add to this, but they are harder to predict and matter less.

Darwin admitted that no one has yet given a definition of a species that satisfies every naturalist, yet people still use the word with a rough shared understanding. Good working terms can stay useful even when their exact edges are disputed.

Darwin noted that individual differences within one species are common, and that even important-looking parts vary. He warned that people who assume important features never vary are arguing in a circle.

Darwin observed that experts often dislike finding variation in what they consider key traits, so they seldom examine internal organs across many specimens. Careful, patient checking often shows more variety than expected.

Darwin observed that when two forms are linked by intermediate examples, scientists usually class one as a variety of the other. He warned that assumptions about missing links open a wide door to doubt and guesswork.

Darwin held that when judging whether a form is a species or a variety, the opinion of experienced, sound-judging experts is the best guide. Where they disagree, a majority view is often the practical answer.

Darwin noticed that experts often disagree on whether a form is a species or a mere variety, so the line between them is vague and arbitrary. Ask two careful judges and you may get two different answers.
Darwin held that arguing over whether a doubtful form is a species or a variety is pointless until the terms are clearly defined. Settle what you mean by the words before you argue about the answer.

Darwin weighed a case from many angles, such as appearance, habitat, range and crossing, and found the evidence pointing in different directions. Judge a hard question by gathering several kinds of evidence, not by one striking feature.

Darwin observed that the things people care most about get studied most, and so they collect the most disputed labels. Close, patient investigation usually brings careful people to agreement in the end.

Darwin observed that a beginner tends to make too many species, because they are impressed by small differences and lack wider knowledge. Only by studying widely does one learn to tell varieties from species, and even then at the cost of admitting more variation.

Darwin held that there is no clear dividing line between species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences, which blend into one another in an unbroken series. Each slight difference can be seen as a first step towards a more marked one.

books.title: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci
books.author: Leonardo da Vinci
books.subject: art
books.licence_note: Author died 1519, translator died 1937. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Richter observed that a hard task can still be mastered with practice and patience, even when the method looks awkward or backwards at first.
Leonardo da Vinci worked as an enquirer, testing things one by one through detailed research. He never gathered his findings into order, which left his notes in confusion.

Leonardo da Vinci held that each observation should be finished on the page where it began. Richter notes that a clear final arrangement can still be built from scattered material if each part is well defined.

Leonardo's notebooks can be put in order by their dates and page layout, and a numbered index lets a reader trace each passage back to its place in the original. Checking where a note came from keeps the record trustworthy.

Copies made from copies drift away from the original, and a compiler who leaves the order unsettled hands the mess on to every later editor. Go back to the source where you can, and do not adopt someone else's arrangement without checking it.

The editor gained access to the original manuscripts by asking owners and institutions directly and thanking them for their help. Careful research depends on patient requests and on being open about who helped you.

Leonardo's genius is judged to lie in his restless curiosity across many fields, not in a squandering of effort. The editor argues that his studies needed centuries of work just to begin to explain them.
Leonardo's principles often agreed more with later science than with his own contemporaries. Good thinking can be ahead of its time and be recognised only when others catch up.
Leonardo meant to arrange his scattered notes by subject before publishing them. The notes were a working collection, and the job of sorting them was a discipline in its own right.
Leonardo held that a painter needs theoretical knowledge of how the eye works, not just skill with the brush. Understanding the reasons behind what you see makes the craft sounder.
Leonardo da Vinci treated careful observation as the basis of skill, testing how distance, light and shade change the way things look before drawing them.
Leonardo da Vinci studied nature closely, noting how light, shade and wind change a tree, so that his work rested on watching the real thing.
Leonardo da Vinci held that an artist must work with industry and thoroughness, and that a painter should learn anatomy and study widely rather than only one narrow skill.
Leonardo da Vinci advised a student to choose his company carefully and to plan his time for study, so that daily habits support the craft.
Leonardo da Vinci held that a useful science should always include its application and use, so that the knowledge does not end up useless.
Leonardo da Vinci admitted that his notes were a disordered collection, and he meant to sort them later by subject, so a messy first draft is fine if you plan to tidy it.
Leonardo da Vinci separated theory from practice when arranging his work, so each proven principle came first and its practical uses followed, keeping the whole coherent.
Leonardo da Vinci ordered his teaching from simple cases to complex ones, starting with simple beams before moving to supported and suspended ones.
Leonardo da Vinci held that a man of wisdom values the food of the mind above material riches, and that the soul's possessions outrank those of the body.
Leonardo da Vinci held that experience, rather than borrowed words, is the true mistress of those who write well, so he would rely on observed evidence over quotation.

Leonardo da Vinci held that inventors and interpreters of nature deserve more esteem than those who only repeat the works of others, and that trusting pure experience beats deferring to reputed authority.
Leonardo da Vinci held that the certainty of mathematical demonstration lifts the mind, and he planned to set out his ideas in short, ordered steps that move from causes to effects and back again.
Leonardo da Vinci held that a picture needs both convincing depth and varied, purposeful action in its figures, so that the people shown do not all look alike.
Leonardo da Vinci held that practice must be founded on sound theory, since a painter who works by eye alone without reasons is like a sailor with no rudder or compass.
Leonardo da Vinci held that knowing your own mistakes lets you correct them and avoid repeating them, and that sound judgment grows from clear understanding built on tested experience.
Leonardo da Vinci held that we should not accept old authorities on matters that can be checked, and should test claims against our own careful observation and experience.

Leonardo da Vinci held that painting rests on the attributes of sight, such as light, shade, colour, form, position, distance and motion, and that a painter must master these to imitate nature. Looking at a thing closely and carefully is the basis of good work.

Leonardo da Vinci noticed that a flat picture seen with one eye can look like real relief, while seen with both eyes it does not. The lesson is that how you look at something changes what you perceive.

Leonardo da Vinci observed that a shadowed place looks darker when you step in from bright light, because the eye adjusts to the light it has just been in. Judge a thing by what you see after your eyes have adjusted, not by the glare you came from.
Leonardo da Vinci noticed that the eye takes time to adjust when moving between bright and shaded places, so it cannot see well right away. He learnt this from a painting he had made of an eye.

Leonardo da Vinci suggested a simple test: hold a candle near a star and lower it slowly, and the star seems to fade as the light grows. The point is that what we see depends on the light around us as well as the thing itself.

Leonardo da Vinci held that perspective is the best guide to painting, and that it makes flat things look raised and raised things look flat. Good work starts with understanding how the eye actually sees.
Leonardo da Vinci used the camera obscura to explain how the eye forms images, which gave painters a way to build a true picture of depth from observation rather than guesswork.

Leonardo built his account of perspective on the basic terms of geometry: point, line, angle, surface and solid. He insisted that a point is not part of a line, so the simplest parts must be clear before the harder problems can be solved.

Leonardo held that a line has no substance and is closer to an imagined idea than a physical thing. Study the outline of every object closely, noting whether its curves are arched convexities or angular concavities.

Leonardo advised painters not to surround bodies with hard lines, since outlines blur at a distance and the parts of small objects vanish. Show edges through light and shade rather than drawn borders.

Leonardo described perspective as a reasoned way of showing that every object sends its image to the eye through a pyramid of lines converging at one point. Bodies of equal size look smaller as they recede because their pyramids shrink.
Leonardo da Vinci held that the eye takes in an object clearly only when its image lies along the central line of sight, so we must turn the eye from letter to letter to read a row of them.

Leonardo da Vinci argued that every visible object sends its lines to the eye in a pyramid meeting at one indivisible point, so a tiny object seen from afar keeps its size rather than shrinking into a speck.
Leonardo da Vinci observed that the eye is a poor judge of distance between objects of equal size, and that a vertical plane, the standard of perspective, is needed to judge them correctly.
Leonardo da Vinci taught that the nearer a cut is made across the pyramid of sight, the smaller the image of the object appears, which is the basis for drawing true size on a flat surface.

Leonardo da Vinci held that the eye judges both how far away an object is and in which direction it lies, and both must be read together, kept on the same level. Objects on a flat ground seem to rise toward the eye with distance but never rise above the eye's own level.

Leonardo da Vinci suggested a simple test of perspective: walk beside a ploughed field and watch the straight furrows seem to draw together toward a point in the distance. That meeting point is the vanishing point that moves as you move.

Leonardo da Vinci showed that you can measure distance by sliding a rod back and forth until its ends line up with a tower's ends, then noting how the image shrinks as the rod is brought nearer the eye. Judging size by comparison with a known object works without any instruments.
Leonardo da Vinci held that every body fills the surrounding air with images of itself, so each small part of the air carries the whole form of the object it comes from.
Leonardo da Vinci's method was to test a claim against a concrete example, such as a light between two mirrors, before trusting it.
Leonardo da Vinci observed that two facing mirrors reflect each other endlessly, a small example of how many images can share the same space without mixing or blocking one another.
Leonardo da Vinci reasoned that the eye sends its own image out to the objects in front of it while taking in their images, which is why seeing is a two-way exchange through the air.

Leonardo da Vinci observed that images of objects spread through the air in every direction, so that every point of a scene is present in every part of the air. He tested this with pinholes in a dark chamber.

Leonardo da Vinci argued that the eye does not send out a visible ray to reach the sun, since such a ray would take time to travel and would be bent by the wind. Seeing happens instantly and undisturbed, so the eye must receive images rather than project them.

Leonardo da Vinci reasoned that if objects sent their images to the eye, they would shrink as they lost material. He proposed instead that the air itself draws in the images of things, like a loadstone, and so the nature of the medium matters as much as the object.

Leonardo observed that a small hole in a wall lets light from a sunlit scene project an upside-down image onto the opposite wall. Every point of the scene reaches every part of that wall, so the picture is complete in each small piece.

Leonardo held that the eye works like a darkened chamber with a small opening, where images cross and arrive upside down. He tested this by letting sunlit objects pass through a pinhole onto white paper inside a dark room.

Leonardo noted that light bends when it passes from thinner air into denser water or glass, so objects seen through water appear out of their true place. He used this to explain why the eye's judgment of position can mislead.

Leonardo da Vinci reasoned from experiment: if you shift one edge of a small hole in a dark room, the image moves, because light travels in straight lines and each edge decides which rays get through. Careful observation of how a simple setup behaves can reveal how light works.

Leonardo da Vinci held that every point of a line can be treated as a point, so a whole circle's image can meet at one point without the rays getting in each other's way. Working through a problem by breaking it into its simplest parts can make a hard idea clear.

Leonardo da Vinci argued from first principles that a line has no thickness, so two sides of it cannot cross each other. Testing an idea by moving the parts in your head and checking what must follow is a sound way to think.

Leonardo da Vinci observed that the narrower the opening, the closer to the opening the light rays cross each other. Small changes to the size of an opening change the whole pattern, so look closely at how each part of a system shapes the result.

Leonardo da Vinci observed that an image cannot be seen between the object and the opening that admits its light, since the air there is not visibly lit. He also noted that where images overlap they look darker.

Leonardo da Vinci described perspective as seeing objects through a flat transparent plane, such as glass, and drawing what the eye sees on it. Each object is traced along lines running to a single point in the eye.

books.title: The Wealth of Nations
books.author: Adam Smith
books.subject: economics
books.licence_note: Author died 1790. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Adam Smith held that a nation's supply of goods depends on two things: how skilfully and wisely its labour is applied, and how many of its people are doing useful work compared with those who are not.

Adam Smith held that the skill and method with which work is done matters more to a society's abundance than the sheer number of people working, and that a frugal, hard-working person can gain more than the poorest societies could give.

Adam Smith held that a nation's yearly supply of goods depends on how many people are doing useful productive work compared with those who are not. The more capital put to work, the more productive labour it sets going.

Adam Smith held that the biggest gains in what labour can produce come from dividing work into separate parts, with each worker doing one piece. The division is often easiest to see in small trades, where all the workers can be watched in one place.

Adam Smith showed with the pin factory that splitting a job into many small distinct operations, each done by a practised hand, multiplies what a group can produce far beyond what the same people could manage working alone.
Adam Smith held that the division of labour raises productive power in every trade, and that the more advanced a society becomes, the more each person tends to do just one part of the work.

Adam Smith noted that farming resists this kind of splitting, since the seasons call for the same workers to do many different tasks, which is one reason farm productivity improves more slowly than manufacturing.
Adam Smith argued that each country tends to gain most from making the goods that suit its own soil, climate and situation, since those goods can then be made better and cheaper than elsewhere.
Adam Smith held that dividing work into simple steps raises output in three ways: workers get more skilled, less time is lost switching tasks, and machines get invented.
Adam Smith noticed that switching between different tasks wastes time and dulls focus, since a person who keeps changing jobs seldom applies full effort to any of them.
Adam Smith observed that people who focus on one simple task are more likely to find easier methods for it, so many useful improvements come from the workers doing the job.

Adam Smith observed that improvements to machines often come from the makers of machines and from thinkers who watch closely, and that dividing intellectual work into branches makes each person more skilled and saves time.
Adam Smith held that when each worker specialises and produces more than they need, trading the surplus with others spreads plenty through every rank of society.

Adam Smith showed that even a plain woollen coat depends on the work of many people, from shepherds and carriers to dyers and weavers, so everyday goods reflect a web of cooperation most of us never see.
Adam Smith argued that even the humblest person's household goods rely on the combined skills of thousands, so we should not underrate how much we depend on others.
Adam Smith held that the division of labour grows slowly from a natural human urge to trade and exchange, not from anyone planning the wealth it later creates.

Adam Smith held that we get most of what we need from others by appealing to their self-interest rather than their kindness, so a good offer says: give me what I want and you shall have what you want.
Adam Smith observed that people in civilised society need the help of great numbers of others, while their own lives are enough to win only a few real friends.

Adam Smith held that people specialise because they can trade their surplus for what they need, so the certainty of exchange is what encourages each person to develop a particular skill to a high level.

Adam Smith argued that many differences in talent between adults grow out of habit, custom and training after childhood, rather than being fixed by nature, and that the division of labour widens them.

Adam Smith observed that differences in talent only help people when they can exchange what they make, since animals of one species with different skills gain little from each other without a way to trade.

Adam Smith held that the division of labour is limited by the size of the market, since a person can only specialise if he can trade his surplus for what he needs. A small market keeps people doing many jobs themselves.

Adam Smith observed that a trade can only support full-time work where there are enough customers nearby, so a village workman must do many kinds of work. Specialists thrive in towns and places with more buyers.

Adam Smith showed that water transport opens a far wider market than land carriage, so industry grows first along coasts and navigable rivers. Cheap transport is what lets a business reach enough customers to specialise.

Adam Smith argued that trade between distant places depends on the cost of moving goods, and cheap transport lets each place become a market for the other. Lowering the cost of reaching customers widens what can be sold profitably.

Adam Smith held that markets grow outward from the sea and great rivers, so the inland parts of a country improve later, since their market is only the land around them. Cheap transport opens the whole world to a producer.

Adam Smith observed that early civilisation grew around the calm Mediterranean, where fear of open water kept navigation close to shore. Safe, sheltered routes let trade and skill spread before people dared bolder voyages.
Adam Smith saw that Egypt's many canals let goods and people move cheaply between towns, villages and farms, and he thought this easy inland trade was a main cause of its early improvement.

Adam Smith noted that Bengal and eastern China grew rich through their dense networks of inland waterways rather than through foreign trade. Making it cheap to move goods nearby can build prosperity on its own.
Adam Smith noted that land far from the sea or from navigable rivers stays poor in trade, and that a river running through another territory can be blocked by whoever controls its mouth.
Adam Smith observed that once labour is divided, most of a person's needs are met by trading the surplus of their own work for what others produce, so everyone becomes a kind of merchant.

Adam Smith saw that barter stalls when the person with spare goods cannot find someone who wants what they have to offer in return. Every prudent person therefore keeps a stock of something others are likely to accept.
Adam Smith argued that metals suit money because they keep well, can be divided without loss and be joined back together, so a buyer can pay the exact amount needed.

Adam Smith held that a public stamp on coins saves everyone the trouble of weighing and testing metal, which makes trade faster and fairer. Without it, buyers were open to cheap fakes that looked like the real thing.

Smith's point is that a trusted, standard mark lets people accept value without checking every detail themselves. Good certification, in any trade, cuts the cost of doing business and protects honest sellers and buyers alike.

Smith observed that the names of old coins, like the pound, first described a set weight of metal before they became mere labels. Over time a unit's name can drift away from the real thing it once measured, so it is worth asking what a standard truly stands for.

Adam Smith observed that when rulers quietly reduce the metal in their coins, debtors gain and creditors lose, since debts are paid back in the same nominal sum. Watch out for loose money, as it quietly shifts wealth from lenders to borrowers.

Adam Smith drew a useful split between value in use, what a thing is good for, and value in exchange, what it will buy. The two often run in opposite directions, as water is vital yet cheap while a diamond is nearly useless yet costly.

Adam Smith was willing to be tedious in order to be clear, and he admitted that abstract subjects may stay hard even after careful explanation. For any hard idea, it is worth taking the time to explain it fully rather than rushing.
Adam Smith held that a person is rich or poor according to how much other people's labour they can command or afford to buy, since few needs can be met by one's own work once trade is divided up.

Adam Smith held that the true cost of anything is the toil and trouble of getting it, and that money and goods are really stored labour exchanged for other labour. Before money, labour was the first price paid for everything.
Adam Smith held that wealth is really the power to command other people's work and its produce, so a fortune is worth exactly the amount of labour it can buy.

Adam Smith held that labour is the true measure of value, but since hardship and skill are hard to measure exactly, prices are settled by rough bargaining in the market, which is good enough for ordinary business.
Adam Smith observed that once money is the common medium of trade, people judge the value of everything by its price in money, since that is the figure they meet first in daily dealings.

Adam Smith held that money itself changes in value, so it makes a poor fixed measure. He argued that the real worth of anything is the labour it costs to acquire, which stays steady for the person doing the work.

Adam Smith distinguished the real price of labour, meaning the goods and necessities a worker can buy with it, from its nominal price in money. He taught that a worker is rich or poor according to the real price.

Adam Smith held that a money rent can lose its value over time, so a family wanting a steady income should not fix it as a set sum of coin. Tying it to a quantity of goods or metal protects it better.
Adam Smith observed that a fixed amount of coin can buy less as the value of the metal it holds falls. Long-term agreements should be wary of this slow erosion.
Adam Smith showed that rents fixed in corn kept their worth far better than rents fixed in money over the centuries. Payments linked to a real good hold up better than a fixed sum of currency.

Adam Smith warned that repeatedly changing the official denomination or metal content of coins can shrink old money debts almost to nothing. Anyone owed a fixed sum should watch for this kind of hidden loss.

Adam Smith observed that the everyday money price of a commodity can stay steady for decades while its price moves sharply from year to year. Short-term swings can hide a steady underlying level, so judge prices over the long run.

Adam Smith held that labour is the only universal and accurate measure of value, since it lets us compare what things are really worth across different times and places. Money measures value well only at the same time and place.

Adam Smith noted that a merchant trading between distant places need only consider the difference between the money he pays and the money he will receive. Real value differences abroad matter less to him than the margin he earns.

Adam Smith noted that people attend mainly to the money price of goods, yet to judge real value across times and places you must compare what the money could buy in labour, not just the silver amount.
Adam Smith observed that a trading nation tends to keep using the metal it first adopted as money for its measure of value, even after the original need for it has passed.

Adam Smith pointed out that people often keep counting their wealth in an old unit, so accounts can outlast the coins they once described, and a debtor's offer in a different form could be refused or accepted on agreed terms.

Adam Smith explained that when the government fixes a legal exchange rate between two metals, the difference between the standard metal and the other becomes little more than a name while that rate holds.

Adam Smith observed that which metal seems the true measure of value depends on which one people use for keeping accounts and writing debts. The metal named in everyday contracts is the one that looks steady.

Adam Smith held that when a coin's value is fixed by law against another metal, the most valuable metal in it effectively sets its worth. Coins that are worn or made of cheap metal still pass at face value, so people judge them by the good metal behind them.
Adam Smith explained that when the mint takes bullion without charging a fee, the coin price becomes the fixed benchmark for the metal. Market prices tend to settle around that benchmark.
